meta.titre: Thermal physics: heat, specific heat capacity and changes of state
meta.sous_theme: heat energy, latent heat and expansion

sections.contenu_markdown: Every morning in Bafoussam a woman heats water on a gas stove for her family's tea, and a baker watches the loaf rise and the oven door swell slightly as the metal warms. Heating things up, melting ice, boiling water and watching materials expand are all examples of thermal physics. The GCE asks short calculations on the heat needed to warm a substance or to change its state, and short explanations of why water is used to cool engines or why a pressure pot cooks faster, so a clear method gains many marks.

items: Energy is measured in joules and power is the energy supplied per second, measured in watts.
Temperature is measured in degrees Celsius or kelvin, and a change of temperature has the same value in both.
Solids, liquids and gases are made of particles, and the arrangement of the particles is different in each state.

sections.titre: Heat, specific heat capacity and the equation for thermal energy
sections.contenu_markdown:
**Heat needed to change the temperature.** The thermal energy $Q$ gained or lost by a body of mass $m$ whose temperature changes by $\Delta\theta$ is

$$Q=mc\,\Delta\theta$$

where $c$ is the **specific heat capacity**: the energy needed to raise the temperature of $1\ \mathrm{kg}$ of the substance by $1\ \mathrm{K}$ (unit $\mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$). For water, $c=4200\ \mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$. Here $\Delta\theta$ is **final minus initial** temperature, never the final temperature alone, and $m$ must be in kilograms.

**Heat capacity** of a whole object, $C=mc$, is the energy needed to raise its temperature by $1\ \mathrm{K}$ (unit $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$). A $0.5\ \mathrm{kg}$ aluminium pan with $c=900\ \mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$ has $C=0.5\times900=450\ \mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$.

**Electrical heating.** If all the electrical energy goes into the substance, $Pt=mc\,\Delta\theta$, so the time needed is $t=\dfrac{mc\,\Delta\theta}{P}$.

**Why water is a good coolant.** Water has a very large specific heat capacity, so it absorbs a large quantity of heat for a small rise in temperature. This is why it cools car engines and is used in hot-water bottles. It is also cheap, safe and easy to find.

**Particle explanation of heating.** When a body is heated its particles gain kinetic energy, vibrate more strongly (solids) or move faster (liquids and gases), and so the body is hotter.

variantes.nom: Change of state and latent heat
variantes.quand_utiliser: When a substance melts, freezes, boils or condenses, so its temperature stays constant.
variantes.contenu_markdown:
During a change of state the temperature stays constant: the energy supplied breaks the attractions between particles instead of raising their kinetic energy. Use

$$Q=ml$$

where $l$ is the **specific latent heat** (energy to change $1\ \mathrm{kg}$ of the substance from one state to another without a change of temperature, unit $\mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}}$). For ice, $l_f=336\,000\ \mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}}$; for water changing to steam, $l_v=2.26\times10^{6}\ \mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}}$ (these values are normally given). **Boiling** takes place throughout the liquid at a fixed temperature, **evaporation** only at the surface and at any temperature. In a **pressure pot** the pressure above the water is higher, so the water boils at a temperature higher than $100\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and the food cooks faster.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When a hot body is mixed with a cold body and you must find the final temperature.
variantes.contenu_markdown: If no heat is lost to the surroundings: **heat lost by the hot body = heat gained by the cold body**. Write $m_1c_1(\theta_1-\theta)=m_2c_2(\theta-\theta_2)$ and solve for the final temperature $\theta$, which lies between the two starting temperatures.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When asked why a material changes size when heated, or about its uses and dangers.
variantes.contenu_markdown: When heated, the particles vibrate or move more strongly and take up more space, so solids, liquids and gases expand (gases most, solids least). Dangers: gaps are left between sections of railway lines and bridges so they do not buckle in the sun. Uses: a **bimetallic strip** (two metals joined) bends when heated because one metal expands more, and is used in thermostats and fire alarms.

sections.enonce_markdown:
An electric kettle rated $2000\ \mathrm{W}$ contains $1.5\ \mathrm{kg}$ of water at $20\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. Take $c=4200\ \mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$ and assume that all the electrical energy is used by the water.

(a) How much heat is needed to bring the water to $100\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, and how long does this take?

(b) The kettle is left on. How much extra time is needed to turn $0.10\ \mathrm{kg}$ of the boiling water into steam? (Specific latent heat of vaporisation $=2.26\times10^{6}\ \mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}}$.)

etapes.justification: The water goes from $20\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ to $100\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$; take final minus initial.
The temperature changes and the state does not.

etapes.action: Find the heating time from the power.
Use $Q=ml$ for the water changing to steam.
etapes.justification: The temperature stays at $100\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ so $mc\Delta\theta$ does not apply; use the latent heat.

sections.conclusion_markdown: **(a)** $Q=504\,000\ \mathrm{J}$, taking **$252\ \mathrm{s}$**. **(b)** An extra **$113\ \mathrm{s}$** is needed to vaporise $0.10\ \mathrm{kg}$ of water.

items.pourquoi_faux: The energy depends on the change of temperature. The water already started at $20\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

items.erreur_markdown: “Ice at $0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ melting needs $Q=mc\,\Delta\theta$ with $\Delta\theta=0$, so no energy is needed.”
items.pourquoi_faux: Energy is needed to change the state even though the temperature does not change. It is used to separate the particles.
The unit of $c$ contains kilograms, so the mass must also be in kilograms. Using grams makes the answer 1000 times too large.

items.erreur_markdown: “Heat capacity and specific heat capacity are the same thing.”
items.pourquoi_faux: Heat capacity ($\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$) belongs to a whole object. Specific heat capacity ($\mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$) is for $1\ \mathrm{kg}$ of a material.

items.erreur_markdown: “Solids expand when heated because their particles become bigger.”
items.pourquoi_faux: The particles keep the same size. They vibrate with larger amplitude and take more room between them.
items.correction_markdown: On heating, the particles vibrate more strongly and move slightly further apart, so the material expands.

items.enonce_markdown:
(a) Calculate the heat needed to raise the temperature of $2.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ of water from $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ to $75\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. ($c=4200\ \mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$)

(b) Why are small gaps left between the rails of a railway line?
items.solution_markdown:
(a) $\Delta\theta=75-25=50\ \mathrm{K}$.

$Q=mc\,\Delta\theta=2.0\times4200\times50=$ **$420\,000\ \mathrm{J}$**.

(b) Steel rails **expand when heated** by the Sun; the gaps give them room to expand so that they do not buckle.

items.enonce_markdown: A student pours $0.50\ \mathrm{kg}$ of water at $80\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ into $1.5\ \mathrm{kg}$ of water at $20\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ in an insulated container. Calculate the final temperature of the mixture and the heat lost by the hot water. ($c=4200\ \mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$)
items.solution_markdown:
Heat lost = heat gained: $0.50\times4200\times(80-\theta)=1.5\times4200\times(\theta-20)$.

The $4200$ cancels: $0.5(80-\theta)=1.5(\theta-20)$, so $40-0.5\theta=1.5\theta-30$, so $70=2\theta$.

$\theta=$ **$35\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$**.

Heat lost by the hot water $=0.50\times4200\times(80-35)=$ **$94\,500\ \mathrm{J}$**.

items.enonce_markdown:
An electric heater of power $1000\ \mathrm{W}$ is used to melt $0.20\ \mathrm{kg}$ of ice at $0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and then to warm the water formed to $30\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. Assume no heat is lost. (Specific latent heat of fusion of ice $=336\,000\ \mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}}$; $c$ of water $=4200\ \mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$.)

(a) Calculate the energy needed to melt the ice.

(b) Calculate the energy needed to warm the water from $0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ to $30\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

(c) How long does the whole process take?

items_markdown: Thermal energy for a temperature change: $Q=mc\,\Delta\theta$ with $\Delta\theta$ = final minus initial and $m$ in kg; water has $c=4200\ \mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$.
Heat capacity $C=mc$ (unit $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$); electrical heating: $Pt=mc\,\Delta\theta$ if there are no losses.
During a change of state the temperature stays constant and $Q=ml$ is used instead.
Method of mixtures: heat lost by the hot body equals heat gained by the cold body.
Water is a good coolant because of its large specific heat capacity; a pressure pot raises the boiling point so food cooks faster.
Solids, liquids and gases expand on heating because their particles move more and take more room.
